name: ECU_Hacker
request:
I want to make my own CAN analyser terminal/app to work with my CAN analyser based on this app HUD ECU Hacker and it's associated custom Candlelight 2.5 firmware. I use it for development and robotics so I have no need for the automotive/car specific features. Here is a link to the firmware that the CAN analysers use: https://github.com/Elmue/CANable-2.5-firmware-Slcan-and-Candlelight and the documentation: https://netcult.ch/elmue/CANable%20Firmware%20Update/#Firmware_Manual and https://netcult.ch/elmue/HUD%20ECU%20Hacker/.

I want to be able to flash and update the analysers from the app, the same as with HUD ECU Hacker. You should use Rust for the app.

last_reply:
I'll first check the native decompiler on this program directly, then make one more pass for the part that's still estimated (the bit-timing search).The timing values are stored by 0x060009f5 (type 0x020000ae). Looking at that type and who calls it:0x060009f1 uses 40, 500, 800 and 900 and calls the two small methods (0x06000a0e/0x06000a0f) that do division by 100 — this looks like the timing calculator. Reading all three:These two work out percentage errors (actual minus wanted, divided by wanted, × 100). Now the main routine 0x060009f1:Now updating the connection code's message and the samplepoint input ranges to match HUD's limits:All 8 tests pass, and HUD's timing method now reproduces the manual's worked example digit for digit. Updating the mechanics sheet:I opened the original's main program and ran Ghidra's pseudocode on it, but the only machine code in it is a one-line hand-off to .NET (`_CorExeMain`). Everything else is scrambled .NET code, so I decompiled that at the instruction level instead. By tracing where the app stores the baudrate settings it sends to the adapter, I found HUD's own baudrate and sample-point calculator: 0x060009f1 runs the search and 0x06000a12 tries one prescaler, with small helpers for the error and comparison steps.

The app now uses HUD's exact method:
- **Speed calculation:** time units per bit = CAN clock ÷ prescaler ÷ baudrate. Segment 1 + 1 = time units × sample point ÷ 1000, and segment 2 is the rest.
- **What's rejected:** anything with fewer than 3 time units per bit, or a baudrate more than 0.5% off.
- **How the best is picked:** the smallest baudrate error first, then the smallest sample-point error. Prescalers are tried from 1 upward, shared between the normal and CAN FD speeds, stopping at the first exact match (both errors under 0.01%).
- **Allowed sample points:** 50–90% for the normal speed and 50–80% for the CAN FD data speed; the input boxes now stop at these limits.

It reproduces the firmware manual's worked example exactly (prescaler 2, segments 139/20 for the normal speed and 29/10 for the data speed). All of this is in the mechanics sheet with the method addresses. The app builds, all 8 self-tests pass, and it passes the check.

Two small steps in that calculator I couldn't pin down, so they are marked as estimated:
- **The 88% check:** I couldn't tell what it does, so I left it out.
- **The synchronisation setting:** it is set to the smaller of the two segments, as in the firmware's sample code.

It still hasn't been tried with a real adapter.
